steps.text:
## 1.1. Technical Debt

The idea of technical debt (TD) as a metaphor was introduced by Ward Cunningham more than 30 years ago. The exact definition of the term varies a bit, but there is a reasonable consensus that TD is a “collection of design or implementation constructs that are expedient in the short term, but set up a technical context that can make future changes more costly or impossible”. Over time, even though it has its inherent limitations, the TD metaphor has gained acceptance and is widely used by both academics and practitioners.

Researchers have identified different types of TD and have tried to categorize them. One study, for example, identifies eight different dimensions of TD, which include code, design and architecture, operational processes, and others. Similarly, another study and a third one each distinguish between 15 different types of TD, for example design debt, code debt, test debt, and documentation debt.

TD by definition has advantages and disadvantages. The advantages that are reported are mostly increased short-term developer velocity. The disadvantages that are reported are decreased long-term velocity, reduced developer morale and motivation, and also lower code quality and more uncertainty and risk.

Besides conceptual considerations, qualitative studies, and surveys, researchers have become more and more interested in doing large-scale quantitative studies on TD with data that is mined from software repositories.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## 1.1. Technical Debt

The idea of technical debt (TD) as a metaphor was introduced by Ward Cunningham more than 30 years ago. The exact definition of the term varies a bit, but there is a reasonable consensus that TD is a “collection of design or implementation constructs that are expedient in the short term, but set up a technical context that can make future changes more costly or impossible”. Over time, even though it has its inherent limitations, the TD metaphor has gained acceptance and is widely used by both academics and practitioners.

Researchers have identified different types of TD and have tried to categorize them. One study, for example, identifies eight different dimensions of TD, which include code, design and architecture, operational processes, and others. Similarly, another study and a third one each distinguish between 15 different types of TD, for example design debt, code debt, test debt, and documentation debt.

TD by definition has advantages and disadvantages. The advantages that are reported are mostly increased short-term developer velocity. The disadvantages that are reported are decreased long-term velocity, reduced developer morale and motivation, and also lower code quality and more uncertainty and risk.

Besides conceptual considerations, qualitative studies, and surveys, researchers have become more and more interested in doing large-scale quantitative studies on TD with data that is mined from software repositories.

## 1.2. The Technical Debt Dataset and its Limitations

To make such studies of TD possible, prior work developed the “Technical Debt Dataset” (TDD). It is a dataset of TD, mostly code debt, in different Apache Software Foundation (ASF) projects that are written in Java. It has been used in a variety of studies on TD. The most recent version is 2.0, and it contains a comprehensive analysis of the main branches of 31 projects. It has data from PyDriller, Refactoring Miner, Jira, and Ptidej, but most notably the dataset includes TD information that was generated with SonarQube.

The important thing is that SonarQube needs the build of a commit to complete before it can give TD information. But builds can fail for various reasons, for example deficient code or missing dependencies. So the TDD does not have complete information for such commits. Our own analyses showed that the SonarQube analyses were incomplete for more than 60% of commits in the projects that are covered.

Recent research found that this is especially a problem when differences in TD between commits are of interest, because then if information is missing in either the focal commit or its parent commit, the data is missing in the final analysis. This problem has been reported to reduce sample sizes dramatically, which can impact the validity of the analyses done on them. For example, in a recent study on developer personality and TD, the authors collected personality data for 121 developers who made commits within the scope of the TDD, but they could only use data from 19 developers because TD information was missing in the TDD.

Also, it is well-known that different TD detection tools can come to different assessments of TD. Since the TDD only has TD items from SonarQube, it is naturally limited in this way as well.

Researchers have identified different types of TD and have tried to categorize them. One study [5], for example, identifies eight different dimensions of TD, which include code, design and architecture, operational processes, and others [5]. Similarly, another study [6] and a third one [7] each distinguish between 15 different types of TD, for example design debt, code debt, test debt, and documentation debt [6,7].

The disadvantages that are reported [9] are decreased long-term velocity [8], reduced developer morale and motivation [10,11,4], and also lower code quality and more uncertainty and risk [5].

Besides conceptual considerations [3], qualitative studies [10], and surveys [9], researchers have become more and more interested in doing large-scale quantitative studies on TD with data that is mined from software repositories [12,13,14,15].

To make such studies of TD possible, prior work [16] developed the “Technical Debt Dataset” (TDD) [16]. It is a dataset of TD, mostly code debt, in different Apache Software Foundation (ASF) projects that are written in Java. It has been used in a variety of studies on TD [12,13,14,15]. The most recent version is 2.0, and it contains a comprehensive analysis of the main branches of 31 projects. It has data from PyDriller, Refactoring Miner, Jira, and Ptidej, but most notably the dataset includes TD information that was generated with SonarQube.

Recent research found that this is especially a problem when differences in TD between commits are of interest, because then if information is missing in either the focal commit or its parent commit, the data is missing in the final analysis. steps.text:
## 1.1. Technical Debt

The metaphorical notion of technical debt (TD) was introduced by Ward Cunningham more than 30 years ago [1]. Despite slight variations in the exact definition of the term, there is reasonable consensus that TD is a “collection of design or implementation constructs that are expedient in the short term, but set up a technical context that can make future changes more costly or impossible” [2]. Over time, despite its inherent limitations [3], the TD metaphor has gained acceptance and is widely used in both academic and practitioner circles [4].

Researchers have identified different types of TD and tried to categorize them. [5], for example, identify eight different dimensions of TD, including code, design and architecture, and operational processes, among others [5]. Relatedly, [6] and [7] each distinguish between 15 different types of TD, such as design debt, code debt, test debt, and documentation debt [6,7].

By definition, TD comes with advantages and disadvantages. Reported advantages lie mainly in increased short-term developer velocity [8]. Reported disadvantages [9] are decreased long-term velocity [8], reduced developer morale and motivation [10,11,4], and lower code quality and increased uncertainty and risk [5].

Beyond conceptual considerations [3], qualitative studies [10], and surveys [9], researchers have become increasingly interested in performing large-scale quantitative studies on TD using data mined from software repositories [12,13,14,15].

## 1.2. The Technical Debt Dataset and its Limitations

To enable such studies of TD, [16] developed the “Technical Debt Dataset” (TDD) [16]. It is a dataset of TD (primarily code debt) in various Apache Software Foundation (ASF) projects written in Java, and it has been used in a variety of studies on TD [12,13,14,15]. Its most recent version 2.0 contains a comprehensive analysis of the main branches of 31 projects. Aside from data obtained from PyDriller, Refactoring Miner, Jira, and Ptidej, the dataset most notably includes TD information generated with SonarQube.

Importantly, SonarQube requires the build of a commit to complete before it can provide TD information. However, builds may fail for various reasons (e.g., deficient code or missing dependencies), and the TDD consequently does not contain complete information for such commits. According to our own analyses, the SonarQube analyses were incomplete for more than 60% of commits in the covered projects.

Recent research has found this to be particularly problematic when differences in TD between commits are of interest, because missing information in either the focal commit or its parent commit then leads to missing data in the ultimate analysis. This problem has been reported to reduce sample sizes dramatically, potentially impacting the validity of the analyses performed on them. For instance, in the recent study on developer personality and TD by [17], the authors collected personality data for 121 developers who made commits within the scope of the TDD, but could only use data from 19 developers due to missing TD information in the TDD [17].

Further, it is well-known that TD detection tools may come to different assessments of TD [18]. As the TDD only contains TD items from SonarQube, it is naturally limited in this way as well.
